issue.title: Harbour Runtime — self-hosted Node.js runtime for the browser
issue.description:
**Status: In Progress — Phase E (migration) in flight.** Research (HAR-371) + contract closure (HAR-370) and **Phases A–D (HAR-440 → HAR-443) are Done.** Phase E (HAR-444) is decomposed E1/E2/E3: **E1 wire+validate (HAR-490) Done**; **E2 flip-default (HAR-491) Done — the boot default is now** `harbour` **as of 2026-05-25 (commit** `91c8038`**,** `src/runtime/index.js:14`**)**; **E3 retire-WC (HAR-492) Todo** — the only remaining concrete step, gated on a stability window from the (not-yet-cut) `harbour-runtime-default-v1` release tag. Gate-discovered hardening is tracked under HAR-589 / HAR-545 / HAR-497, not by reopening phase tickets.

This is an **epic** — the actual work lives in the five phase subtasks. This issue's body documents the current strategy, architecture, and constraints. Per-phase design happens inside each subtask when it's picked up.

---

## TL;DR

Replace `@webcontainer/api` with a self-hosted Node.js-compatible runtime built on **Web Workers + OPFS + a Service Worker networking bridge**, hidden behind a `HARBOUR_RUNTIME` selector flag so the migration is reversible. The boot default flipped to `harbour` on 2026-05-25 (HAR-491 / Phase E2) after Harbour-real cleared the "Claude Code boots and runs" bar; `HARBOUR_RUNTIME=webcontainers` remains a fully-supported rollback opt-out until WC is retired in E3 (HAR-492).

The strategy moved three times before settling — see **Historical context** at the bottom. The current position (post HAR-371 research, May 2026) is **build from scratch, conformance-driven, peers as design references not bases**.

## Why

* **No CDN dependency at boot.** Eliminates StackBlitz multi-MB WASM fetch.
* **\~100ms cold-start** vs 2–5s with WebContainers — near-instant restart, dissolves HAR-146-class cold-boot problems.
* **Full ownership.** Debuggable in DevTools, no vendor pricing risk, no proprietary lock-in.
* **Broader browser support.** Removes SharedArrayBuffer / COOP / COEP requirement → Safari and static-hosting unblocked.
* **Harbour's accumulated shim/shell knowledge is reusable as-is.** The shims patch Node, not WebContainers (see 2026-04-21 comment *Runtime abstraction*).

## Architecture

```
src/core/runtime-adapter.ts                 # Typed contract — HAR-371 / HAR-438 deliverable
src/runtime/
  index.js                                  # Selector — reads HARBOUR_RUNTIME at boot
  webcontainers/index.js                    # createAdapter() — wraps @webcontainer/api  (current default)
  harbour/index.js                          # createAdapter() — Workers + OPFS + SW       (HAR-149 deliverable)
test/fixtures/fake-runtime.ts               # Third adapter — conformance-tested baseline
test/unit/runtime-adapter-conformance.test.ts   # Parameterised over all three adapters
```

### Selection — boot-time, one runtime per session

`HARBOUR_RUNTIME` is a migration flag, not a per-call switch. The default is now `harbour` (flipped in HAR-491 / E2, 2026-05-25); `webcontainers` is the reversible rollback opt-out, preserved verbatim until E3 (HAR-492) retires it.

```js
// vite.config.js
export default defineConfig({
  envPrefix: ['VITE_', 'HARBOUR_'],
  // ...
});

// src/runtime/index.js
const name = import.meta.env.HARBOUR_RUNTIME ?? 'harbour'; // default flipped to harbour in HAR-491 (E2)
```

## Phases

Detailed design happens inside each subtask. The phases are deliberately the shape of the original proposal (March 2026) — the work decomposes cleanly along these boundaries. Every phase is gated by the conformance suite (`test/unit/runtime-adapter-conformance.test.ts`).

| Phase | Subtask | Exit criterion |
| -- | -- | -- |
| **A — Foundation** | HAR-440 | `require('express')` resolves inside a Worker |
| **B — Networking** | HAR-441 | Iframe loads an Express app via the SW bridge |
| **C — Build tools** | HAR-442 | `npx vite` boots a React dev server |
| **D — Package management** | HAR-443 | `npm install express` succeeds in-runtime |
| **E — Migration** | HAR-444 | Default flag = `harbour`, `@webcontainer/api` removed |

## Constraints (probe-confirmed)

From HAR-437 (`docs/wc-probe-report.md`). These are the load-bearing WC behaviours Harbour-real must reproduce — or explicitly fix and paper over inside the WC adapter:

* **inv #4** Bare spawns inherit `HOME=/home`, `PATH=/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin`, `COLORTERM=truecolor`.
* **inv #6** `proc.input.getWriter().close()` does **not** propagate EOF — embed payloads in argv when EOF matters.
* **inv #15** `proc.input.getWriter()` holds an exclusive lock — share one writer across the process lifetime.
* **inv #23** Exit codes 0 and 143 are "clean"; everything else is a crash.
* **inv #24** Drain `proc.output` before awaiting `proc.exit` or the process deadlocks under backpressure.
* **Probe finding** Mount-tree top-level keys resolve under `/home/<workdirName>/`.
* **Probe finding** `proc.kill()` (no signal) resolves with exit **127**; `proc.kill('SIGKILL')` with **143**.
* **Probe finding** `port` close fires *before* `proc.exit` resolves for the owning process.
* **Probe finding** The `wc.mount(tree, { mountPoint })` option is non-functional in WC ^1.5.1.

Six **other** HAR-435 invariants were contradicted by the probe (env replace, argv newline, mount-after-spawn invisibility, `wc.fs.writeFile` host-only, mount clobber, `fs.watch` sync ENOENT). Harbour-real **does not need to reproduce** any of them. Their cleanup in current code is tracked separately — see HAR-445.

## Match-or-fix decisions (deferred to per-phase tickets)

For each probe-confirmed wart, Harbour-real picks: inherit (smaller contract) or fix (cleaner DX, but the WC adapter must paper over). The interesting cases:

| WC behaviour | Match → cheaper | Fix → stronger |
| -- | -- | -- |
| `writer.close()` no EOF | Argv-only workaround (HAR-325) survives | Delete the inline-script gymnastics across `wc-fs-helpers`, `auth-config`, `FileBrowser`, `shim-log-poller` |
| `proc.output` backpressure | Drain-before-await rule everywhere | Bounded async streams; drain-or-await orthogonal |
| `proc.kill()` default → 127 | Capture as-observed | Surface a sensible default (SIGTERM=143) |
| `port` close before `proc.exit` | Preserve (ProcessManager depends on it) | Same — must preserve or UI breaks |
| Mount-tree home-prefix | Inherit the implicit resolution | Explicit `bindWorkspace(uuid)` — HAR-436 decomp #10 |
| `workdirName` not enforced across boots (HAR-336) | Same — identity by convention | **First-class snapshot identity** — UUID as primary key. The one place Harbour-real is genuinely stronger than WC. |

## Acceptance criteria

* All five phase subtasks (HAR-440 → HAR-444) complete.
* `runtime-adapter-conformance.test.ts` passes for both `webcontainers` and `harbour` factories simultaneously.
* Full bundled-app suite passes against `HARBOUR_RUNTIME=harbour`.
* **Claude Code boots, completes a non-trivial agent task, and the user can't tell which runtime they're on.** This was the gating bar for the default flip (done 2026-05-25, HAR-491/E2). It now gates E3 (WC retirement) and the cutting of the `harbour-runtime-default-v1` stability tag, not the flip itself.
* `@webcontainer/api` removed from `package.json`.
* Documentation (`docs/architecture.md`, `harbour-os/CLAUDE.md`) updated to reflect the new runtime as default.

## Nested Harbour OS — design implications

(Full mapping in the 2026-04-19 comment.) HAR-149 dissolves three WC-imposed blockers (single-instance, page-level COI, COEP iframe partitioning) and introduces/leaves three others to design in:

1. **Service Worker scope collision** — outer SW intercepts nested fetches unless routes carry a frame/instance token (e.g. `/__hr/<instance-id>/...`). Design in during Phase B.
2. **Origin/opener leakage** — OAuth popup flow, proxy URL resolution, broker channels all currently assume single-tenant.
3. **OPFS partitioning** — each Harbour instance needs a virtual FS root scoped by frame identity. Design in during Phase A.

These are not Phase A–E blockers but should be designed in early. File follow-up tickets as they surface.

## Follow-ups (filed separately)

* **HAR-445** — Delete the 6 dead WC workarounds surfaced by HAR-437 probe (cleanup, not a HAR-149 phase — applicable against current WC or opportunistically during Phase E).

## Out of scope

* Multi-runtime per session (one runtime per page).
* Native modules / N-API (out of scope for any browser runtime).
* Backwards compatibility with WC-only public APIs not on the adapter contract (`wc.export` snapshot blobs, recursive `wc.fs.watch`) — replaced by OPFS-native equivalents in Phase A.

---

## Historical context

The strategy moved three times. Preserving the trajectory so the rationale isn't lost — and so a future reader knows why the description doesn't say "fork almostnode" anymore.

### 2026-03-31 — Original proposal: build from scratch

Web Workers + Service Worker bridge + in-memory FS persisted to IndexedDB. Tiered module strategy (Tier 1 pure-JS as-is, Tier 2 polyfills, Tier 3 stubs, Tier 4 build). Phases A–E. Justification: full ownership, no CDN, ~100ms boot, Safari support, no COOP/COEP. Full design doc at `docs/harbour-runtime.md`.

### 2026-04-19 — Landscape review: fork-and-extend

Two viable MIT-licensed bases surfaced (almostnode 1.1k★, Lifo 485★). OPFS sync access handles became universally supported. Reframe: "~90% of the benefits for a fraction of the effort. Harbour's moat is the agent-native OS, not the runtime."

### 2026-04-20 — Recalibration: build from scratch with peers as references

Hands-on review against the "Claude Code boots" bar disqualified both candidate bases. almostnode stubs `child_process`; Lifo claims it but doesn't solve shell-level semantics Harbour has already fixed (HAR-242 / HAR-236 / HAR-259 / HAR-306 / HAR-257). Forking either means inheriting their gaps + porting Harbour's shell/shim lineage on top — not obviously cheaper than starting from a cleaner foundation.

### 2026-05-23 — Strategic synthesis after HAR-371 phase 4

Contract surface is ~10–12 primitives, not 21. Lifo is the constraining shape, not WC — designing for Lifo gives Harbour-real generous headroom. Six HAR-435 invariants don't actually hold in WC ^1.5.1 (probe-confirmed) — fewer workarounds to reproduce. Conformance suite (HAR-438) is the development truth-table from day one.

---

## Phases F + G added (2026-06-18)

Phase E (HAR-444) bundled flag-flip + validation + retire-WC. Flip+validation are done (E1/E2); the remaining work was split into two new phases so each has one crisp goal:

* **Phase F (HAR-676)** — real apps run on real Harbour end-to-end via any install mechanism (App Store, URL, CLI, git, npm, upload). Gate: HAR-554. Owns the product acceptance bar. In Progress.
* **Phase G (HAR-677)** — retire & remove WebContainers (delete `@webcontainer/api` + importers + WC adapter + conformance row + docs). Owns the original E3 (HAR-492). **Blocked by Phase F** + the stability window.

Phase sequence is now A–G.

## Nested Harbour OS — feasibility mapping

Feasibility check on running Harbour OS inside Harbour OS today (on WebContainers) surfaced six gaps. HAR-149 dissolves the three platform-level hard blockers but introduces/leaves three others that should be designed-in.

### What HAR-149 resolves

| Gap (on WebContainers) | Why it goes away |
| --- | --- |
| Single WebContainer instance per page (`@webcontainer/api` constraint) | Apps already run per-Worker; nothing limits runtime-per-page |
| Cross-origin isolation not per-iframe (`crossOriginIsolated` inherits from top) | Explicitly in scope — "removes SharedArrayBuffer requirement" |
| `COEP: credentialless` partitions nested iframe storage | Goes away with COI removal |

### What HAR-149 does **not** resolve (or makes worse)

**1. Service Worker scope collision (worse).** HAR-149 relies on a Service Worker as the virtual-networking bridge. Browsers allow one active SW per scope, so a nested Harbour OS at the same origin cannot register its own — the outer SW intercepts all nested fetches.

*Design implication:* the SW needs to multiplex by frame identity. Routes should carry a frame/instance token (e.g. `/__hr/<instance-id>/...`) and dispatch to the right handler table. The outer OS mints the token when creating the nested iframe, and the inner OS registers its virtual servers under that namespace.

**2. Origin/opener leakage.** OAuth popup flow (`github-auth-bridge.js`), proxy URL resolution (`boot-provisioning.js:25-29`), and anything keying off `window.location.origin` / `window.opener` assume top-level frame semantics. A nested frame at the same origin collides with the parent.

*Design implication:* frame-scoped identity instead of origin-scoped identity for auth callbacks, proxy routing, and postMessage targets.

**3. Boot provisioning is single-tenant.** Hardcoded workdir pinning, single MCP bridge polling `~/.harbour-os/mcp-requests/`, and shared auth config would corrupt shared state across nested instances.

*Design implication:* per-instance virtual FS root and per-instance MCP bridge paths. HAR-149's in-memory FS tree + IDB persistence makes this easier than today — each instance can hold its own tree.

### Suggested addition to scope

A "Nested instances" sub-section in the design doc covering:
- SW route namespacing by frame/instance token
- Per-instance FS root (already natural with HAR-149's architecture)
- Frame-scoped OAuth + MCP bridge paths

None of these are large, but they're easy to bake in early and hard to retrofit.

## Follow-up — recalibration after hands-on review

Spent time with Lifo and almostnode. The landscape review above overweighted star counts as a maturity signal; the real picture is narrower.

### Running Claude Code is the actual bar, and neither passes it

almostnode stubs `child_process` outright — Claude Code can't spawn `node`/`npx`/`rg`/`git`, so it won't boot. Lifo claims `child_process` but doesn't appear to have solved shell-level semantics that Harbour has already fixed: stable `cd` across chained commands (HAR-242), correct `$?` propagation (HAR-236), `>&2` redirects (HAR-259), escape marker reassembly across stream chunks (HAR-306, still open here too), `.harbour-apps/bin/` PATH discovery (HAR-257). A real agent workload hits these within minutes.

This reframes the competitive map. The set of browser runtimes that actually run production agent workloads is currently Harbour + WebContainers — not the 2,000+ combined stars implied.

### What this changes for this issue

The fork-and-extend framing above was too optimistic:

* **Both candidate bases are thinner than their star counts suggest.** Forking either one means inheriting their gaps while also needing to port Harbour's accumulated shell/shim knowledge on top. That's not obviously cheaper than starting from a cleaner foundation.
* **Harbour's shim + shell bug lineage is a compounding asset.** Every HAR-23x/24x/25x/30x fix is a specific thing an alternative base will re-encounter. That knowledge belongs in the Workers/OPFS core we build, not grafted onto a fork that hasn't learned it.
* **almostnode and Lifo are better treated as design references than forks.** Study their Service Worker bridge, module loader wiring, and OPFS usage. Don't inherit their stubs or their unsolved shell bugs.

### Revised direction

Build our own, slowly closing the gap against WebContainers — not a big-bang replacement. The path:

1. **Start narrow.** Workers + OPFS + Service Worker bridge + module loader, sized to run one known-good bundled app end-to-end (Vite + React preview in an iframe).
2. **Port shim knowledge directly** — the HAR-23x/24x/25x/30x fixes go into the runtime's core as it lands, not retrofitted later.
3. **Keep the feature flag migration path.** `HarbourRuntime.boot()` and `WebContainer.boot()` live side-by-side behind ProcessManager. Apps migrate one at a time.
4. **Let Claude Code run be the acceptance test** — not module coverage percentages. If the bundled agent boots, does tool calls, and completes a real task against the new runtime, we're shipping.

This keeps HAR-149's original ambition intact — full ownership, no CDN, debuggability, Safari support — while accepting that the work is genuinely ours to do rather than mostly-done-by-someone-else.

**Suggestion: add `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent` to the Step 1 bundled-app boot test.**

Context: investigating an install failure today on `pi-coding-agent@0.68.0` inside WebContainer. The package installs fine but crashes on first run with:

```
SyntaxError: The requested module './core/sdk.js' does not provide an export named 'AgentSessionRuntime'
  at ModuleJob._instantiate (builtins.*.js) — WebContainer internal
```

The package itself is valid — it runs cleanly on native Node 22 (its declared engine is `>=20.6.0`). The failure is in WebContainer's ESM linker. Tracing the module graph in `dist/`:

- `index.js:16` → `export { AgentSessionRuntime, … } from './core/sdk.js'` (named re-export)
- `core/sdk.js:17` → `export * from './agent-session-runtime.js'` (star re-export — where the class actually lives)
- `core/extensions/loader.js:23` → `import * as _bundledPiCodingAgent from '../../index.js'` — closes the cycle

Full cycle: `sdk.js` → `agent-session.js` → `extensions/index.js` → `loader.js` → `index.js` → `sdk.js`. V8 resolves `AgentSessionRuntime` through the star chain correctly; WebContainer's linker doesn't. Same class of failure as pi-mono #2452 (`@mariozechner/pi-tui` — `getEditorKeybindings`), since fixed upstream by expanding the star.

**Why this is worth including in the spike:**

Pi is built with the modern TS-barrel output pattern that stresses every major part of an ESM linker in one package — cyclic imports, `export * from` re-exports, `import * as ns`, and dynamic `jiti`-based extension loading. It's deliberately aggressive about the module graph. Passing the bundled-app suite tells you the happy path works; passing Pi tells you the linker is probably done.

Concrete asks on this ticket:

1. Add `npm i -g @mariozechner/pi-coding-agent && pi --help` to the Step 1 boot test matrix (almostnode and Lifo).
2. If either fails, capture the exact linker-resolution step that breaks — that's the diff-vs-V8 to characterise.
3. If both pass, it's a strong signal the fork's module loader handles real-world TS barrel code without further work.

Short-term workaround (separate from HAR-149) is an upstream PR on `badlogic/pi-mono` expanding the `export *` in `src/core/sdk.ts` — same shape as the pi-tui #2452 fix. Noting here for completeness; unblocks users today regardless of runtime timeline.

## Runtime abstraction — notes from codebase analysis

Deep-dive into the current codebase surfaces several findings that aren't yet captured in this issue.

### The minimal runtime contract

The issue identifies ProcessManager as the swap point but doesn't define exactly what the runtime needs to expose. From examining every call site, Harbour's actual usage is:

```
interface Runtime {
  spawn(cmd, args, { env, cwd }) → { input, output, exit, kill, resize }
  fs.readFile / writeFile / readdir / rm / watch
  mount(tree)             // batch write shortcut
  on('server-ready', …)  // port detection
  on('port', …)
  on('error', …)
}
```

That's the complete surface. WebContainers provides a full POSIX kernel (fork, signals, `/proc`, libuv, the works) and Harbour uses almost none of it. The custom runtime only needs to be this interface — not a Linux kernel.

### Shim portability

The shims patch Node.js APIs, not WebContainers APIs — they are runtime-agnostic. On a custom runtime:

**Shims that survive unchanged:**
- `network-shim` — patches `fetch`/`http.request`, routes via CORS proxy, enforces domain consent
- `env-shim` — proxies `process.env`, enforces per-key consent
- All bin shims (`bash`, `git`, `npm`, `curl`, `grep`, etc.) — pure JS, no WC dependency

**Shims that disappear entirely:**
- `spawn-shim` — exists solely to fix two WebContainers bugs (vendored ELF binary redirection, broken FD stdio arrays). On a runtime we control, these are implemented correctly from the start.
- `fs-monitor` — patches fs writes to detect changes for persistence. On a custom runtime, this belongs in the fs layer directly.

This means the shim surface *shrinks* with a custom runtime, not grows.

### The three abstraction leaks

ProcessManager is described as the swap point, but three places currently bypass it and call `getWebContainer()` directly:

1. `network-consent-store.js` + `env-consent-store.js` — write policy decisions via a spawned Node process
2. `FileBrowser.jsx` — `readdir`, `readFile`, `rm` calls
3. `provision.mjs` + `provision-bundled-apps.mjs` — provisioning scripts

These need routing through the RuntimeAdapter before any swap is viable. Scoped change — all four call sites are straightforward.

### The one WC-specific gap

`fs-persistence.js` uses `wc.export('.', { format: 'binary' })` for snapshot export — a WebContainers-specific API with no generic equivalent. On a custom runtime, snapshots come from OPFS directly (which is actually simpler). This needs an explicit plan before Phase E (migration).

### Recommended prerequisite: RuntimeAdapter interface

Before the empirical spikes (almostnode/Lifo), worth defining a `RuntimeAdapter` duck-type (~20 lines) and closing the three leaks. This:
- Makes the spike results directly comparable (both adapters implement the same contract)
- Bounds the migration blast radius precisely
- Confirms ProcessManager really is the complete swap point

No implementation risk — it's naming what already exists and patching three call sites.

## Strategy synthesis & entry-point confirmation (2026-05-23)

Research pass over the description (2026-03-31), the four comments (Apr 19 → Apr 21), and the two subtasks (HAR-371, HAR-370). This issue's framing has moved twice; documenting the trajectory here so the next action is unambiguous.

### 1. Strategy evolution — three distinct positions

| # | Date | Position | Rationale | What changed next |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| **1. Original proposal** | 2026-03-31 (description body, *Original proposal* section) | **Build from scratch.** Phases A–E. Web Workers + Service Worker bridge + in-memory FS persisted to IndexedDB. | Full ownership, no CDN, ~100ms boot, Safari support, no COOP/COEP. | Three weeks later a landscape review surfaced two viable forkable bases. |
| **2. Landscape review** | 2026-04-19 (description body, *Update — April 2026* section) | **Fork-and-extend.** Prefer almostnode (250KB, 40+ shims, no `child_process`) or Lifo (15 shims *including* `child_process`, but less mature). OPFS now universally supported. | "~90% of the benefits for a fraction of the effort. Harbour's moat is the agent-native OS, not the runtime." | Hands-on review against the "run Claude Code" bar disqualified both. |
| **3. Recalibration** | 2026-04-20 (comment: *Follow-up — recalibration after hands-on review*), reinforced 2026-04-21 (comments on `pi-coding-agent` boot test + Runtime abstraction analysis) | **Build from scratch — peers as design references, not bases.** Workers + OPFS + Service Worker bridge + module loader, narrow start (one bundled app end-to-end), port Harbour's HAR-23x/24x/25x/30x shell/shim fixes directly into the core. Acceptance = Claude Code (and pi-coding-agent) boots and completes a real task. | This is the current strategy. The description body still reflects position #2 and is now stale. |

**What flipped between #2 and #3:** the landscape review weighted star counts as a maturity signal. Hands-on confirmed almostnode stubs `child_process` outright (Claude Code can't spawn `node`/`npx`/`rg`/`git`) and Lifo hasn't solved shell-level semantics Harbour has already fixed (HAR-242 chained `cd`, HAR-236 `$?`, HAR-259 `>&2`, HAR-306 escape-marker reassembly, HAR-257 PATH). Forking either base means inheriting their gaps *and* re-porting Harbour's accumulated shell knowledge on top — not obviously cheaper than building on a cleaner foundation. The HAR-23x/24x/25x/30x lineage is reframed as a *compounding asset* that belongs in the runtime core, not as something to graft onto someone else's fork.

**What survived all three positions:** the original motivation (full ownership, no CDN, debuggability, Safari support) and ProcessManager as the swap point.

### 2. Entry-point confirmation: HAR-371 is the unblock

The Apr 21 *Runtime abstraction* comment identified the minimal runtime contract Harbour actually consumes (spawn / fs.{read,write,readdir,rm,watch} / mount / on('server-ready'|'port'|'error')) — much smaller than WebContainers' full POSIX kernel — and flagged three abstraction leaks where call sites bypass ProcessManager:

1. `src/stores/network-consent-store.js` — `getWebContainer()` for consent/policy writes
2. `src/stores/env-consent-store.js` — same shape
3. `src/components/FileBrowser.jsx` — `manager._wc` for readdir/readFile/rm
4. `src/system-tools/provision.mjs` (+ `provision-bundled-apps.mjs`) — raw `wc` parameter

The original Apr 21 recommendation was a ~20-line duck-typed `RuntimeAdapter`. HAR-370's planning session (see its Apr 22 comments) then rescoped: a 20-line structural seam is **not** a behavioural contract — at least 9 implicit contracts live outside the signatures (process shape, event signatures, mount-tree grammar, FS-layer semantics, jsh assumption, NODE_OPTIONS shims, port→iframe wiring, filesystem conventions, env-replace-not-merge). A spike against a thin seam would "work" for a near-clone of WC and fail silently for anything genuinely different.

That insight produced **HAR-371** — research + typed contract + conformance suite + FakeRuntime + behavioural probe of WC. HAR-370 was rescoped to leak closure *only*, blocked by HAR-371.

**Confirmed sequencing:**

```
HAR-371 (contract + conformance + WC probe)
   ↓ blocks
HAR-370 (leak closure — applies typed contract from HAR-371)
   ↓ unblocks
HAR-149 (build the runtime against the contract, peer-runtimes as design references)
```

## Strategic synthesis after HAR-371 phase 4 (2026-05-23)

The four research phases (HAR-434 inventory, HAR-435 invariants, HAR-436 peer-gap, HAR-437 probe — all Done) sharpen the picture of what "build our own runtime" actually entails. Folding the load-bearing implications into this ticket so HAR-149's design pressure is captured explicitly rather than living only in chat.

### 1. The contract surface is smaller than it looks

74 inventory rows collapse to 21 unique primitives. 10 are flagged for decomposition. Strip the optional capabilities (symlink, `preview-message`, `resize`, snapshot-blob extraction) and the **minimum required surface for HAR-149 is ~10–12 primitives**. That's a tractable target — and it's bounded by the contract (HAR-438), not by HAR-149's ambition.

### 2. Lifo is the constraining shape, not WC

Of 21 primitives, **13 are `✗ missing` on Lifo's host SDK** (per `docs/runtime-peer-gap.md`). WC and almostnode are close to each other shape-wise; Lifo is fundamentally different — buffered exec, no streaming output, no host-side stdin, no kill, no `fs.watch`, no `mkdir/rm/readdir`, no port events.

If the contract must accommodate Lifo (the explicit research goal), it has to sit at a very low layer. **This means HAR-149 gets the easy job:** if we design for Lifo, every primitive Lifo can't do, our runtime can. The contract's lowest common denominator is generous to anyone building above it. The hard work is on HAR-438 (contract author), not on us when we build HAR-149.

### 3. Six "load-bearing" invariants are folklore in this WC build

The probe (HAR-437) revealed that **6 of the 29 invariants enumerated in `docs/runtime-contract-invariants.md` don't actually hold against `@webcontainer/api` ^1.5.1**:

- inv #1 (mount-after-spawn invisible) — process **DID** see the late mount
- inv #2 (`wc.fs.writeFile` host-only) — process **DID** read the host write
- inv #3 (mount clobber) — re-mount **composes** at per-file level, doesn't clobber siblings
- inv #5 (env replaces wholesale) — env **merges** with WC defaults
- inv #19 (argv `\n` becomes `'n'`) — newline **preserved** verbatim
- inv #14 (`fs.watch` ENOENT sync throw) — returns handle, **async** error

See `docs/wc-probe-report.md` §6 for full evidence. The probe confirmed the other 5 load-bearing invariants (#4, #6, #15, #23, #24).

**The implication for HAR-149 is liberating, not constraining.** Half the workarounds in `process-manager.js` are coding around behaviours WC either never had or no longer has. Our runtime doesn't need to reproduce them. The strict list of constraints HAR-149 **must** preserve is what the probe **confirmed**, not what HAR-435 documented.

### 4. Some warts are real — match or fix is HAR-149's call

For each WC behaviour the probe **confirmed**, HAR-149 gets to pick — match (inherit the wart, simplest contract) or fix (cleaner DX, but WC adapter + FakeRuntime must paper over):

| WC behaviour | Match (inherit) | Fix (HAR-149 stronger) |
|---|---|---|
| `writer.close()` doesn't propagate EOF (inv #6, confirmed) | argv-only workaround pattern (HAR-325) survives | Delete HAR-325 inline-script gymnastics across `wc-fs-helpers`, `auth-config`, `FileBrowser`, `shim-log-poller` |
| `proc.output` backpressure deadlocks `proc.exit` (inv #24, confirmed) | Drain-before-await rule everywhere | Bounded async streams — drain-or-await orthogonal |
| `proc.kill()` default → exit 127, `kill('SIGKILL')` → 143 (new, from probe) | Capture as-observed in contract | Surface a sensible default (SIGTERM=143) |
| `port` close fires *before* `proc.exit` resolves (new, from probe) | Preserve order (ProcessManager depends on it) | Same — must preserve or UI breaks (URL revert) |
| Mount-tree rooted at `/home/<workdirName>/`, with auto-home-prefix on `wc.fs.*` | Inherit the implicit resolution | Explicit `bindWorkspace(uuid)` (HAR-436 decomp #10) — cleaner semantics |
| `workdirName` not enforced across boots (HAR-336) | Same — workspace identity is by convention | **First-class snapshot identity** — UUID is a primary key; HAR-149 enforces what WC merely allows |

The last row is the most interesting: it's a place where HAR-149 is genuinely **stronger** than WC, not just substitutable. Worth designing in early.

### 5. The conformance suite is HAR-149's development truth-table

HAR-438 produces `test/unit/runtime-adapter-conformance.test.ts` parameterised over adapter factories. The probe report (`docs/wc-probe-report.md` §8) names the verbatim assertions. **HAR-149 should develop against the conformance suite from day one** — every primitive we land, we run conformance against, and we know we're compatible. The same suite that gates WC, almostnode, and Lifo gates Harbour-real.

Corollary: the probe is pinned to `@webcontainer/api` ^1.5.1. **HAR-149's contract is versioned**, not "whatever WC happens to do today." When StackBlitz ships a minor with breaking semantics, conformance catches it — and we get to decide whether to update the contract or stay pinned.

issue.title: Runtime integration gaps (gate-discovered)
issue.description:
Container for **gaps discovered by gate checks** during the HAR-149 runtime migration — the "oh, we actually need X, go back and add it" work that integration surfaces after a phase has shipped its planned scope.

## Why this exists

The phases (A–E) are a *plan* — a forward decomposition written before building. Gaps are *discoveries* — things integration teaches us that the plan couldn't know. Filing discoveries back into the phase tree (reopening a "complete" phase, scattering one gap's fix across three subtrees) is what made the board hard to read. A plan is a tree; discovered dependencies are a graph that overlays it. Don't force the graph into the tree.

## Convention

1. **A gate-discovered gap lives here**, parented to the epic — never back under a phase, regardless of which subsystem it touches.
2. **It carries a real** `blocks` **edge to the gate that found it** (e.g. the install-pipeline gate HAR-498), so "what's blocking the gate?" is a query, not an archaeology dig.
3. **The phase that shipped stays Done.** "Done" means *delivered the planned scope against then-current knowledge* — not *perfect forever*. New integration debt is a new gap here, not a reopened phase.
4. **A gap can be a mini-epic** (break it down under itself); because it sits at epic level, the depth stays legible.
5. **Supersession is explicit and terminal** — the superseded ticket is Canceled with a `duplicate` edge to its heir, its body reconciled.
6. **The relation graph is the source of truth**; prose roadmaps are derived from it, never hand-maintained alongside it.

issue.description:
> ## ✅ Planner finalized (verified at HEAD `283bde8`, 2026-06-11)
>
> **Session-fit: NEEDS MULTIPLE SESSIONS** (no structural refactor; 3 independently-verifiable units).
> Full plan + dependency arrows + regression constraints in the planner comment dated 2026-06-11.
>
> **Prerequisite (blocks this issue): HAR-621** — export the shared non-shimmed macrotask scheduler from `async-io.js` (currently module-private). Both #1 and #2 build on it.
>
> **Order:** HAR-621 → (#1 shim+alias, additive) ‖ (#2 liveness-seam deferral, core exit path) → remove HAR-612 keepalive (acceptance gate, only after both green).
>
> **Correction to edit-site list:** #2's REPL mirror is `commands/jsh.js:299` (synchronous `activeCount()` read in `runCommand`), NOT `process-global.js`. The three #2 edit sites are `worker-entry.js:961`, `event-loop.js notifyIfDrained` (microtask→macrotask, shared by BOTH loops), and `jsh.js:299`.
>
> **#1 alias gotcha:** existing aliases are bare-name anchored; readable-stream does `require('process/')` WITH a slash — the find must be `/^process\/?$/`, verify it intercepts the trailing-slash specifier.
>
> ---

## Worker liveness misses untracked deferred continuations — two DIFFERENT root primitives

> **Research (2026-06-11, verified at HEAD** `283bde8`**).** Both manifestations exit 0 with empty output before an awaited continuation completes, but they escape through **different** primitives in **different bundling domains**. The ticket's original 'one shared hop, fix npm-`process` nextTick' framing is corrected below. Full trace in the research comment.

### Liveness model (confirmed at HEAD)

`event-loop.js` is an active-handle refcount; a process stays alive while `activeCount()>0`. `worker-entry.js:961` makes the idle-exit decision **synchronously** after `await handler(proc)`. Handles come from the per-spawn timer shim (`timers.js`), fetch tracking, and async-fs ops (`asAsync`→`trackAsyncOp`: synchronous retain, **macrotask** release via `MessageChannel`, HAR-606). `node -e` runs the body synchronously, so an async IIFE kicks off and the check decides exit on what holds a handle.

### #1 — readable-stream deferred `'end'` — PINNED

## Worker liveness misses untracked deferred continuations — two DIFFERENT root primitives

> **Research (2026-06-11, verified at HEAD** `283bde8`**).** Both manifestations exit 0 with empty output before an awaited continuation completes, but they escape through **different** primitives in **different bundling domains**. The ticket's original 'one shared hop, fix npm-`process` nextTick' framing is corrected below. Full trace in the research comment.

### Liveness model (confirmed at HEAD)

`event-loop.js` is an active-handle refcount; a process stays alive while `activeCount()>0`. `worker-entry.js:961` makes the idle-exit decision **synchronously** after `await handler(proc)`. Handles come from the per-spawn timer shim (`timers.js`), fetch tracking, and async-fs ops (`asAsync`→`trackAsyncOp`: synchronous retain, **macrotask** release via `MessageChannel`, HAR-606). `node -e` runs the body synchronously, so an async IIFE kicks off and the check decides exit on what holds a handle.

### #1 — readable-stream deferred `'end'` — PINNED

`readable-stream@4` (Vite-bundled tier2 builtin) → `require('process/')` → npm `process@0.11.10 browser.js`. Its `nextTick` queue is drained by `runTimeout`, which uses `cachedSetTimeout` captured by an IIFE **at module-eval (Worker import phase, before** `handleStart` **installs the timer shim)** = the **native** Worker `setTimeout`. At call time `runTimeout` falls through to `cachedSetTimeout(fun,0)` (browser.js:50) — the **untracked native macrotask**. The deferred `'end'` emission holds no handle; as the only pending work, `activeCount===0` → premature exit. → **untracked NATIVE MACROTASK.**

### #2 — vendored cacache `put` — DIFFERENT root

The **entire** buffer-`put` tree (`cacache`/`minipass@7.1.3`/`minipass-pipeline·flush·collect`/`ssri`/`@npmcli/fs`) has **zero** `setTimeout`**/**`setImmediate`**/**`process.nextTick`; `ssri.fromData` is sync; minipass defers only via `Promise.resolve().then` (**microtask**). Every fs op is individually tracked (`asAsync`, sync retain) and `fs.promises.*` forward to them. So #2 is a **timing race inside harbour's own keepalive bridge** (HAR-606 `MessageChannel` release vs the microtask-dense cacache chain), **not** the npm-`process` mechanism. The exact dipping hop needs runtime counter-instrumentation on the chromium-harbour lane (the implementer's first task). → **internal MICROTASK-bridge race.**

**Bundling separator:** readable-stream is Vite-bundled (alias-reachable); cacache is `require`d from OPFS at runtime (`~/.harbour/vendor/npm/node_modules/cacache`) — **not Vite-bundled**, so a `resolve.alias` cannot reach it. A single bundler/alias fix cannot cover both.

### Substrate witness (already in repo)

`test/e2e/runtime-harbour/har612-crypto-cipherbase.spec.js`: header §2 excludes the `'end'`-await shape (cites this ticket); the cacache section (line 214) carries a load-bearing `setInterval` keepalive commented *'remove when HAR-616 closes.'*

## Recommended approach (TWO coordinated changes)

1. **#1 (additive):** new \~30-line harbour `process` shim + `resolve.alias` (`vite.config.js`) mapping npm `process` → it; `nextTick` retains an event-loop handle, releases on a tracked macrotask (reuse `getActiveEventLoop()`; export `scheduleMacrotask` from `async-io.js` or use `trackAsyncOp`). Mirrors the tier2 alias pattern. **Verify** the alias catches trailing-slash `require('process/')`.
2. **#2 (scoped, liveness seam):** defer the idle-exit *decision* by a full macrotask turn so the cacache chain re-arms its next tracked fs handle before exit is concluded — `worker-entry.js` post-handler check + `event-loop.js notifyIfDrained` (today `queueMicrotask`) + HAR-617 REPL mirror in `process-global.js`. Preserve HAR-606 sync-mode `await` and the green synchronous `crypto.createHash` shapes (they exit synchronously → unaffected). A `MessageChannel`-deferred drain fixes #2 but **not** #1 (ordering), confirming the levers are independent.

**Surface Assessment: implementation can land cleanly on the current code — no structural refactor — but it is two coordinated, independently-verifiable changes, not one. #2 is not a one-liner.**

## Acceptance

* HAR-612 cacache keepalive removed; cacache section stays green.
* Mechanism test: `activeCount` never dips across the `cacache.put` chain; AND awaiting a readable-stream `'end'` as the only pending work exits 0 WITH output.
* No decoy/keepalive patterns (CLAUDE.md liveness lineage: HAR-553/609).

Split from HAR-612 (2026-06-10). Parent HAR-545. Related HAR-553/609/589. Blocks HAR-613. Research verified at HEAD 2026-06-11 (post HAR-617/619).

### Liveness model (HEAD, confirmed)
`event-loop.js` is an active-handle refcount; a process stays alive while `activeCount() > 0`. `worker-entry.handleStart` runs the handler, then makes the idle-exit decision **synchronously** after `await handler(proc)` (worker-entry.js:961): if `activeCount()>0` it arms `onIdle`, else `proc.exit()`. Handles are registered by: the timer shim (`timers.js`, installed per-spawn inside `handleStart`), fetch tracking, and async-fs ops (`asAsync` → `trackAsyncOp`, **synchronous retain**, **macrotask release** via `MessageChannel` — HAR-606). `node -e` runs the script body synchronously (CJS `new Function`), so a `(async()=>{…})()` IIFE kicks off and `wrapped()` returns; the liveness check then decides exit based on what holds a handle.

### Manifestation 1 — readable-stream deferred `'end'` — FULLY PINNED ✅
readable-stream@4 (Vite-bundled tier2 builtin) does `require('process/')` → npm `process@0.11.10` `browser.js`. Its `nextTick` drains a queue scheduled by `runTimeout(drainQueue)`. `runTimeout` (browser.js:38) uses `cachedSetTimeout`, captured by an IIFE **at module-evaluation time** (browser.js:18-37) — which for the Vite worker bundle is the **Worker import phase, BEFORE `handleStart` installs the per-spawn timer shim**. With the `'end'` await as the only pending work, `activeCount()===0` at the check → exit 0, empty output. → **untracked NATIVE MACROTASK.**

**Decisive separator:** readable-stream is **Vite-bundled** (alias-reachable); the vendored cacache is `require`d from OPFS at runtime by absolute path (`~/.harbour/vendor/npm/node_modules/cacache`) through the harbour module-loader — **not Vite-bundled, so a `resolve.alias` cannot reach it.** The two live in different bundling domains.

The ticket's preferred single fix — **option 1, patch npm-`process` nextTick to a tracked scheduler — fixes ONLY #1** (and only because readable-stream is bundled). It cannot touch cacache. Option 2 (wrap native `setTimeout` earlier) also only addresses #1, and is fragile: `runTimeout` calls the *cached reference directly* when it differs from the live global, so re-wrapping the global afterward doesn't help unless the global identity is a stable trampoline captured before the worker imports. **#2 requires a change in the harbour liveness bridge itself**, independent of #1.

1. **#1 (additive):** new ~30-line harbour `process` shim + `resolve.alias` in `vite.config.js` mapping the npm `process` package to it; its `nextTick` retains an event-loop handle and releases on a tracked macrotask (reuse `getActiveEventLoop()`; `scheduleMacrotask` is currently module-private in `async-io.js` and would need exporting, or use `trackAsyncOp`).
